title: The Council at Reinickendorf to the One Word on the Stone: Marcuse, Exile, and the Great Refusal
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Charlottenburg and the Council at Reinickendorf

stops.name: Berlin, the house whose street nobody wrote down
stops.date_confidence: attested; day and year given by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the Frankfurt University Library vita. The street address of the birth is not established in any source consulted, so the coordinate is Berlin city centre, not a building.
stops.campa: A son is born on the nineteenth of July to Carl Marcuse, who deals in textiles, and Gertrud Kreslawsky. The household is Jewish by descent and German by every daily habit, assimilated, comfortable, Prussian, the kind of Berlin apartment where nothing is lacking and the lack of anything lacking is never itself a subject. The Kaiser has been on the throne ten years. The boy is given a name and a class and a city. No source consulted records the street the house stood on.
suggested_refs: The assimilated Jewish Bildungsbürgertum of Wilhelmine Berlin

stops.name: Charlottenburg, the two Gymnasien
stops.date_confidence: attested for the schools and for the span 1911-1916 at the Kaiserin-Augusta-Gymnasium; the Mommsen-Gymnasium years before it are given without dates. Month set to 01 by default. The coordinate is a generic Charlottenburg point standing for both schools, not either building.
stops.campa: He is put through the Mommsen-Gymnasium and then, from 1911, the Kaiserin-Augusta-Gymnasium in Charlottenburg. Greek, Latin, German literature, history: the classical humanistic curriculum designed to produce loyal servants of the state, which in his case produces a reader of Goethe and Schiller who will write his doctorate on the German novel about artists. Neither school building can now be pointed to on the district map with any confidence. He keeps the reading list for sixty years.
suggested_refs: The Wilhelmine Gymnasium curriculum in German literature and the classics

stops.name: Darmstadt, the airship replacement unit
stops.date_confidence: attested for the draft in 1916 and for service away from the front. The two traditions differ on where: German Wikipedia gives a Luftschiffer-Ersatz-Abteilung at Darmstadt and Berlin, assigned on account of an eye condition; the English-language accounts give work connected with horse stables in Berlin. Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinate is Darmstadt.
stops.campa: He is drafted in 1916 and never sees a trench. An eye condition keeps him out of the line, and he is posted instead to a Luftschiffer-Ersatz-Abteilung, an airship replacement unit quartered at Darmstadt and at Berlin. The English-language accounts remember the war differently, as work with horses in a Berlin stable. Whichever it was, he spends it inside Germany, in uniform, while his generation is destroyed at Verdun and on the Somme. The two traditions have never been reconciled.
suggested_refs: Luftschiffer-Ersatz-Abteilungen of the German army, 1916-1918

stops.name: Berlin-Reinickendorf, elected to the soldiers' council
stops.date_confidence: attested for November 1918 by the Frankfurt University Library vita, which also dates his SPD membership from 1917; the day is not recorded and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He has carried a Social Democratic party card since 1917. In November the empire comes apart in a week, sailors first, then garrisons, then the capital, and in Reinickendorf the soldiers of his unit elect him to their council. He is twenty. For a few weeks the ordinary machinery of command is suspended and men who were privates the month before vote on what the army will do. Then the former officers begin standing for election again, and are elected, and the council fills up with the men it was formed against.
suggested_refs: The Berlin soldiers' councils of November 1918

stops.name: Berlin, the canal and the resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested for the murders of Liebknecht and Luxemburg on 15 January 1919; Marcuse's own resignation from the council is [R], reconstructed from recollections he gave in interviews decades afterwards and reported in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. No contemporary letter or document of his fixes the date.
stops.campa: In January the Social Democratic government sets the Freikorps on the revolutionary left. Karl Liebknecht is shot in the Tiergarten. Rosa Luxemburg is beaten, shot, and thrown into the Landwehr canal, and the party that permitted it is the party of his own membership card. Marcuse leaves the council and, with it, the expectation that a workers' party in office will do what a workers' party in opposition swore. He tells the story of this month for the rest of his life. No contemporary document of his fixes the day he walked out.
suggested_refs: The murders of Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, Berlin, 15 January 1919
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Herbert Marcuse', on his later recollections

stops.name: Berlin, four semesters under the lindens
stops.date_confidence: contested year. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy dates the enrolment at the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität to 1919; German Wikipedia dates the same four semesters from 1918, which would place his first term inside the revolution rather than after it. Not resolved here. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He enrols at the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität to read German literature, philosophy, economics and politics, four semesters of them. Politics has just failed in the street and he takes it up at a desk. Outside the building the city runs on soup kitchens, street shootings and an inflation only beginning; inside, the lectures proceed on schedule. He takes no degree in Berlin. In 1920 he packs for Freiburg, three hundred miles south, where the philosophy is done differently.
suggested_refs: The Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität, Unter den Linden, now the Humboldt University

stops.name: Freiburg, the dissertation on the artist-novel
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1922 as the year Freiburg accepted Der deutsche Kunstlerroman; the month is not recorded and defaults to 01. Coordinate is the atlas's existing Freiburg pin, inherited byte-identical from martin_heidegger.journey.json, and sits about two hundred metres from the university's Kollegiengebaude I.
stops.campa: Freiburg accepts a doctoral thesis called Der deutsche Kunstlerroman, the German artist-novel: a study of the figure of the artist in German fiction and of the gap between the work he makes and the society he must live in. It is a literary thesis. The question it puts, whether the thing a person could be has any place to stand inside the arrangement he actually inhabits, is the one he keeps asking in other vocabularies for fifty years. He is twenty-four and signs himself Dr. phil.
suggested_refs: Der deutsche Kunstlerroman (1922), later printed in Schriften vol. 1

stops.name: Berlin, the book trade, Sophie Wertheim, and a son
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage in 1924 and for Peter Marcuse's birth in 1928. The firm he worked for in the book trade and the terms of that employment are not established in any source consulted, an honest gap. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Doctorate in hand, he comes back to Berlin and goes into the book trade, selling and publishing rather than teaching. The same year he marries Sophie Wertheim, a mathematician, who will follow him to Freiburg, Geneva, Paris, New York, Washington, and no further. In 1928 their son Peter is born, the only child Marcuse fathers; he grows up to be a scholar of cities at Columbia. For six years the doctor of philosophy is a Berlin bookseller with a wife and a baby.
suggested_refs: Peter Marcuse (1928-2022), urban planning scholar at Columbia University
sources: marcuse.org family page on Sophie, Inge and Erica, marcuse.org/herbert/people/SophieIngeErica.htm

stops.name: Freiburg, back for Sein und Zeit
stops.date_confidence: contested year. The Stanford Encyclopedia and English Wikipedia give 1928 for the return to Freiburg; the family site marcuse.org dates it 1929. Presented as 1928/29 and not resolved. Month set to order the segment. Freiburg pin inherited from martin_heidegger.journey.json.
stops.campa: Sein und Zeit appears in 1927 and pulls him back south. Marcuse gives up the book trade, returns to Freiburg, and sits in Martin Heidegger's seminars: idealism and realism, truth and certainty, Plato's Parmenides, Kant. Sophie comes to some of the sessions with him. Around Heidegger stands the phenomenological circle that Edmund Husserl built, and around all of it a small Baden university town where the century's most consequential philosophy is being done in rooms that hold thirty people. He intends to habilitate here and stay.
suggested_refs: Heidegger's Freiburg seminar lists, 1928-1932

stops.name: Freiburg, phenomenology and historical materialism
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1928 (Beitrage zu einer Phanomenologie des Historischen Materialismus) and 1929 (Uber konkrete Philosophie), both in the Stanford Encyclopedia bibliography; months not recorded, set to order the segment.
stops.campa: He publishes an essay proposing that Heidegger's analysis of existence and Marx's analysis of capital are describing the same object from two sides, and follows it with a second on what a concrete philosophy would have to be. Both essays take a system built to exclude politics and read the politics back out of it. Nobody in either camp is pleased. The Marxists see a bourgeois mystic; the phenomenologists see a man importing economics into first philosophy. Marcuse holds the position anyway.
suggested_refs: Beitrage zu einer Phanomenologie des Historischen Materialismus (1928)
Uber konkrete Philosophie (1929)
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Herbert Marcuse', bibliography

stops.name: Freiburg, the manuscripts of 1844
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1932 as the year of 'Neue Quellen zur Grundlegung des Historischen Materialismus'; month set to order the segment against the habilitation.
stops.campa: The Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts that Karl Marx wrote in Paris in 1844 and never published are printed for the first time, and Marcuse reviews them within months. He argues that they change everything: that under the economics there was always an account of a human being cut off from his own labour, his own products, and his own kind, and that what looked like a science of prices is a theory of estranged existence. The reading is heresy to the party press in Moscow and is now the standard one everywhere else.
suggested_refs: Neue Quellen zur Grundlegung des Historischen Materialismus (1932), on Marx's 1844 manuscripts
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Herbert Marcuse', bibliography

stops.name: Freiburg, the habilitation that does not happen
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hegels Ontologie und die Grundlegung einer Theorie der Geschichtlichkeit was completed and published in 1932 and that Marcuse never completed a Freiburg habilitation. Whether Heidegger formally rejected the manuscript is disputed and is not resolved here. Month set to order the segment.
stops.campa: He finishes the book meant to open the German professoriate to him, Hegels Ontologie und die Grundlegung einer Theorie der Geschichtlichkeit, a reading of Hegel as a thinker of historical being rather than of the absolute. The habilitation is never completed at Freiburg. Whether Heidegger refused it, or let it die, or simply said nothing, the record does not settle, and Marcuse afterwards told it more than one way. Within a year the racial laws close the German universities to him regardless, and Heidegger joins the party.
suggested_refs: Hegels Ontologie und die Grundlegung einer Theorie der Geschichtlichkeit (1932)

stops.name: Geneva, the branch office and the post taken up
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Institute hired him in 1932 on Leo Lowenthal's recommendation and Max Horkheimer's assessment; he left Germany in May 1933 and took up the post at the Geneva branch, never having worked at the Frankfurt house. Sources that give 1933 for the appointment and 1932 for it are describing two different events. Exact Geneva address not established; coordinate is the city pin already used in max_horkheimer.journey.json.
stops.campa: Leo Lowenthal puts his name forward and Max Horkheimer weighs him up, and the Institute for Social Research takes him on. He never sets foot in it as an employee. In May he leaves Germany, and the post he takes up is at the branch office in Geneva, where the Institute's money already sits, moved out ahead of the seizure of its Frankfurt building. The money is Felix Weil's, made in Argentine grain. A private fortune from Buenos Aires is now paying the salaries of the men who will spend their lives explaining how capital reproduces itself.
suggested_refs: The Societe Internationale de Recherches Sociales, Geneva, holder of the Institute's funds in exile

stops.name: Paris, the journal that keeps its German
stops.date_confidence: attested that Marcuse spent time in Paris in 1933 during the Institute's move and that the Institute's documentation office and its Zeitschrift operated from Paris from 1933; the length and address of Marcuse's own Paris stay are not established. Month set to order the segment. Paris pin inherited from max_horkheimer.journey.json.
stops.campa: He passes some months in Paris, where the Institute has put its documentation office and where the Zeitschrift fur Sozialforschung is printed under a French imprint, in German, for readers who no longer live in Germany. This is the condition of the whole enterprise now: a German journal produced in France with Swiss-held Argentine money for an audience in flight. Nothing in it is stable. How long he stays in the city, and at what address, is recorded nowhere. He writes for the journal from there.
suggested_refs: Zeitschrift fur Sozialforschung, Paris, Felix Alcan imprint, 1933-1939
sources: felix_weil.journey.json, stop on the Ecole normale documentation office

stops.name: Columbia University, Morningside Heights
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1934 as the year of Marcuse's emigration and of the Institute's affiliation with Columbia; month taken from the corresponding stop in felix_weil.journey.json and max_horkheimer.journey.json to keep the shared scene aligned. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from those files.
stops.campa: He crosses with Sophie and Peter and the rest of the exiled Institute: Horkheimer, Pollock, Adorno, Lowenthal, Fromm. Columbia gives them a building on Morningside Heights and the Frankfurt School becomes, for the next fifteen years, a German seminar conducted in upper Manhattan. Marcuse is thirty-six and has no country. He never lives in Germany again and never holds a German chair, and the major books ahead of him are written in a language he learned as an adult.
suggested_refs: The Institute for Social Research at 429 West 117th Street, Columbia University

stops.name: New York, authority, the family, and the postscript
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Studien uber Autoritat und Familie (1936), to which Marcuse contributed the long section on the history of ideas, and for 'Philosophie und kritische Theorie' (1937), written with Max Horkheimer. Months not recorded; defaulted. Columbia coordinate inherited.
stops.campa: The Institute publishes Studien uber Autoritat und Familie, and the long historical section on how obedience got itself argued for is his. The next year he writes with Max Horkheimer the essay that gives the enterprise its name, critical theory: a theory that refuses to be neutral about the arrangement it describes, on the ground that describing it neutrally is one of the ways it is maintained. Which of the two men wrote which paragraphs is recorded in the Frankfurt papers and was not recorded on the title page.
suggested_refs: Studien uber Autoritat und Familie (Paris, 1936)
Philosophie und kritische Theorie (Zeitschrift fur Sozialforschung, 1937)

stops.name: New York, the citizenship and the book on Hegel
stops.date_confidence: attested for naturalization in 1940 and for the publication of Reason and Revolution in 1941. No record of the ceremony or its location was found; the Columbia pin stands for his residence. Months defaulted.
stops.campa: He becomes an American citizen. The following year Reason and Revolution appears, his first book written in English, arguing that Hegel is not the philosopher of the Prussian state that everyone from the liberals to the Nazis has agreed he is, but a thinker of negation, of the refusal of the given. The tradition being invoked to justify the Reich, a refugee tells his new public, contains the instruments for taking it apart. The book comes out while German armies hold Paris.
suggested_refs: Reason and Revolution: Hegel and the Rise of Social Theory (Oxford University Press, 1941)

stops.name: Washington, the Office of War Information and the Research and Analysis Branch
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1942 as the year he went to Washington for the Office of War Information and 1943 for the move to the OSS Research and Analysis Branch; the Frankfurt vita spans the government years as 1942-1950. A dossier claim of 1941 is wrong: he was still at the Columbia Institute that year. Months defaulted. The coordinate approximates the wartime OSS offices; the exact buildings are not confirmed.
stops.campa: He goes to Washington in 1942 for the Office of War Information and moves the next year to the Research and Analysis Branch of the OSS. A room of German emigre scholars, Franz Neumann, Otto Kirchheimer, Felix Gilbert, spends the war reading the Reich for the American government: who holds which ministry, what the party does to the courts, where morale is breaking, how the thing might come apart. Marxists on the payroll of military intelligence. The reports are secret, unsigned, and printed as a book forty years later.
suggested_refs: Secret Reports on Nazi Germany: The Frankfurt School Contribution to the War Effort (Princeton, 2013)
sources: Princeton University Press chapter introduction to Secret Reports on Nazi Germany

stops.name: Washington, the Central European desk
stops.date_confidence: attested that he continued in government analytical work after the OSS was dissolved, including the State Department's Office of Intelligence Research, reportedly heading a Central European section. Sources differ on the end year, the Frankfurt vita giving 1950 and other accounts 1951; not resolved. Month set to order the segment.
stops.campa: The OSS is dissolved and the work continues under the State Department, in the Office of Intelligence Research, where he is said to have run the Central European section. He is now a middle-aged civil servant with a security clearance, writing assessments of the country he was born in for the government of the country that took him in. The FBI has been keeping a file on him since 1943 and will keep it open into the 1970s. Nothing in it ever produces a charge.
suggested_refs: Marcuse's FBI file, opened 1943
sources: 'Under Surveillance: Herbert Marcuse and the FBI', researchgate.net/publication/242335852

stops.name: Todtnauberg, the visit to the hut
stops.date_confidence: attested by marcuse.org's documentary page on the Marcuse-Heidegger relation, which records a visit to Heidegger at Todtnauberg in spring 1947; the exact day is not given and the month is set to order the segment. Coordinate is the atlas's Todtnauberg pin, inherited byte-identical from martin_heidegger.journey.json.
stops.campa: In the spring he climbs to the ski hut in the Black Forest where his old teacher is living out his ban from teaching. Heidegger has been a party member since 1933, has served as rector under the new order, and has said nothing publicly since. Marcuse has spent the war analysing the regime for American intelligence. What the two men said to each other in that room is not recorded by either of them. Marcuse comes down the mountain and, in August, writes.
suggested_refs: Heidegger's hut at Todtnauberg in the Black Forest
sources: martin_heidegger.journey.json, stop 'Todtnauberg, the hut on the slope'

stops.name: Washington, the letters to Freiburg
stops.date_confidence: attested. Three letters are printed at marcuse.org: Marcuse to Heidegger, 28 August 1947; Heidegger to Marcuse, 20 January 1948; Marcuse to Heidegger, 12 May 1948. The demand for a public avowal is in the first, the equation of the murdered Jews with the expelled Germans in the second, and the refusal in the third. The stop is dated to the first letter and covers the exchange.
stops.campa: He asks Heidegger for one thing: a public statement, unambiguous, that he has broken with the regime he joined. Heidegger answers in January by setting the extermination of the Jews beside the postwar expulsion of Germans from the east, as though the two were the same kind of event. In May Marcuse replies that with that sentence Heidegger has put himself outside the dimension in which a conversation between men is even possible, outside the logos. There are three letters in all, and after the third they do not write again. He goes on using the teaching.
suggested_refs: The Marcuse-Heidegger correspondence, 1947-1948, printed in full at marcuse.org

stops.name: Washington, the Freud lectures and the loss of Sophie
stops.date_confidence: attested for the lectures at the Washington School of Psychiatry around 1950-1951 and for Sophie Wertheim Marcuse's death of cancer in 1951, after which he left government service. Months defaulted; the coordinate is the Washington School of Psychiatry, and Sophie's place of death is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: He lectures at the Washington School of Psychiatry on Sigmund Freud, working out the argument that repression comes in two kinds, the amount any civilization requires and the far larger amount required only by this one. In 1951 Sophie dies of cancer. They have been married twenty-seven years, through Freiburg, Geneva, Paris, New York and this city. He leaves the State Department. The book that comes out of these lectures four years later carries her name on the dedication page.
suggested_refs: The Washington School of Psychiatry lectures, seedbed of Eros and Civilization

segments.name: Brandeis: Eros and the One Dimension

stops.name: Columbia University, the Russian Institute
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1952-1953 at Columbia's Russian Institute by the Frankfurt vita; months defaulted. Coordinate is the Columbia pin already canonical in the atlas, although this is a separate and later affiliation from the Institute for Social Research that occupied it in the 1930s.
stops.campa: Fifty-four years old, widowed, out of government, he takes a research post at Columbia's Russian Institute and turns to the other half of the twentieth century's ledger. The Cold War wants Soviet experts; he becomes one, on his own terms, reading the official Soviet philosophical literature in the original the way he had read Hegel. The buildings on Morningside Heights are the ones the exiled Institute sat in twenty years before. The post runs two years.
suggested_refs: Columbia University Russian Institute, founded 1946

stops.name: Cambridge, the Russian Research Center
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1954 at Harvard's Russian Research Center; month defaulted. Coordinate is Harvard Yard. The Center itself sat off the Yard in this period, at 16 Dunster Street and later Coolidge Hall, and the exact address of his desk is not established.
stops.campa: The work moves to Harvard's Russian Research Center, and out of it comes Soviet Marxism, published in 1958: a study of how a doctrine of liberation becomes the official language of a bureaucratic state, and of what happens to concepts when a party owns them. He grants the system a capacity to liberalize that neither the Cold Warriors nor the Communists want to hear about. The Center itself sits off the Yard, on Dunster Street, and which desk was his is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Soviet Marxism: A Critical Analysis (Columbia University Press, 1958)

stops.name: Waltham, the chair at Brandeis
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1954 as the start of the Brandeis appointment; month set to the academic year. Franz Neumann died in a Swiss car accident in September 1954, and Marcuse married his widow Inge Werner Neumann in 1956, the year given by both the Frankfurt vita and the marcuse.org family page. A 1955 date circulates without support in either.
stops.campa: He joins Brandeis, a university seven years old, to teach political theory and the history of ideas; the appointment will last eleven years. His students there include Angela Davis and Andrew Feenberg. In September of the same year Franz Neumann, his closest friend from the OSS room, is killed in a car on a Swiss road. Marcuse marries Neumann's widow, Inge, two years after that, and helps raise her two sons. He is fifty-eight, and it is his second marriage.
suggested_refs: Franz Neumann, Behemoth: The Structure and Practice of National Socialism (1942)

stops.name: Waltham, Eros and Civilization
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1955; month not recorded and defaulted. Erich Fromm's own file dates the reply within Eros and Civilization to the same year, and cites the book directly.
stops.campa: The book appears, dedicated to Sophie. Its claim is that Freud, who thought civilization must cost us our happiness, was right about the mechanism and wrong about the amount: some repression buys the shared world, and the rest buys only the existing order of work and profit. Take away the surplus and a non-repressive civilization becomes thinkable. In an epilogue he turns on Erich Fromm, who has been softening Freud into an ethical preacher, and names him a revisionist. Fromm answers from Mexico City. They do not reconcile.
suggested_refs: Eros and Civilization: A Philosophical Inquiry into Freud (Beacon Press, 1955)
erich_fromm.journey.json, stop dated 1955-01-01, Mexico City
sources: erich_fromm.journey.json, suggested_refs citing Eros and Civilization

stops.name: Waltham, One-Dimensional Man
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1964; month not recorded and defaulted. The quote is verbatim from the Marcuse.org text of chapter 1.
stops.campa: The diagnosis that makes him famous: that advanced industrial society does not need to forbid opposition because it can supply it, absorb it, and sell it back, and that a population which recognizes itself in its cars and its kitchens has no leverage left against the arrangement that issues them, the buyers of this book included. Both the capitalist West and the bureaucratic East are running the same operation. Beacon Press prints it in 1964. It sells in the hundreds of thousands.
stops.quote: A comfortable, smooth, reasonable, democratic unfreedom prevails in advanced industrial civilization, a token of technical progress.
stops.quote_source: One-Dimensional Man (1964), chapter 1, 'The New Forms of Control'
suggested_refs: One-Dimensional Man: Studies in the Ideology of Advanced Industrial Society (Beacon Press, 1964)

stops.name: Heidelberg, the Weber centenary
stops.date_confidence: attested. The fifteenth Deutscher Soziologentag met at Heidelberg in 1964 on the theme 'Max Weber und die Soziologie heute'; Marcuse's paper, 'Industrialisierung und Kapitalismus im Werk Max Webers', was reprinted in Negations (1968). The exact date within the year is not recorded; month set to order the segment. Coordinate is the Heidelberg old town.
stops.campa: German sociology gathers at Heidelberg for the hundredth birthday of Max Weber, and Marcuse comes from Massachusetts to tell it that Weber's formal rationality is not formal. What Weber described as the neutral rationality of the modern enterprise, calculable, impersonal, indifferent to ends, is capitalism's own particular reason wearing the costume of reason as such, and domination is built into the calculation, not added to it afterwards. The paper is called Industrialisierung und Kapitalismus im Werk Max Webers, and Negations reprints it four years later.
stops.quote: And yet this society is irrational as a whole. Its productivity is destructive of the free development of human needs and faculties, its peace maintained by the constant threat of war, its growth dependent on the repression of the real possibilities for pacifying the struggle for existence.
suggested_refs: Industrialisierung und Kapitalismus im Werk Max Webers, in Negations (1968)
sources: de.wikipedia.org, 'Deutsche Gesellschaft fur Soziologie', on the 15th Deutscher Soziologentag

stops.name: Waltham, repressive tolerance and the leaving
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1965 publication of 'Repressive Tolerance' in A Critique of Pure Tolerance and for his departure from Brandeis the same year. The reason for the departure is contested: Angela Davis and others recall a firing for radicalism, while the institutional account is mandatory retirement age with only year-to-year renewal offered. Both are documented; neither is resolved here.
stops.campa: He publishes the essay that will be quoted against him for sixty years: that where power and access are grossly unequal, a tolerance extended equally to every position works to protect the position that already holds the ground, and that neutrality between an established violence and its opponents is not neutrality. The same year he leaves Brandeis. He is sixty-seven, past the retirement age, offered a year at a time. His students say he was pushed. The university says the arithmetic said so.
suggested_refs: Repressive Tolerance, in A Critique of Pure Tolerance, with Robert Paul Wolff and Barrington Moore Jr. (1965)
sources: Logos Journal, 'Marcuse's Most Famous Student: Angela Davis'

stops.name: La Jolla, the chair at the new campus
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1965 as the start of the UC San Diego appointment; month set to the academic year.
stops.campa: The University of California at San Diego is four years old, built on a mesa above the Pacific between a Marine base and the defence laboratories that make Southern California rich. It gives him a chair, and he holds it for five years before he formally retires. He arrives with the manuscript of the decade's most-read attack on exactly this landscape. He will spend the rest of his life in it, in a low house among lemon trees, an hour's drive from the aerospace plants.
stops.quote: The people recognize themselves in their commodities; they find their soul in their automobile, hi-fi set, split-level home, kitchen equipment.
suggested_refs: The founding years of the University of California, San Diego

stops.name: West Berlin, the Henry-Ford-Bau
stops.date_confidence: attested. Marcuse's Berlin lectures of 10-13 July 1967, published as Das Ende der Utopie, were given at the Free University; the coordinate is the Henry-Ford-Bau, whose Audimax held them, rather than the generic FU point. The quote is verbatim from the 1966 Political Preface to Eros and Civilization and is Marcuse reporting a slogan worn on demonstrators' buttons, not a phrase of his own coinage.
stops.campa: He comes back to the city he was born in, which is now half a city, and lectures for four days to the Socialist German Student Union in a packed hall of the Free University. The talks are printed as Das Ende der Utopie: the end of utopia meaning not that hope is finished but that the material conditions for it now exist and the obstacle is no longer scarcity. He argues with Rudi Dutschke. The newspapers begin printing the three Ms, Marx, Mao, Marcuse, and he spends years explaining that he commands nobody.
stops.quote: It is perhaps equally ridiculous and right to see deeper significance in the buttons worn by some of the demonstrators (among them infants) against the slaughter in Vietnam: MAKE LOVE, NOT WAR.
stops.quote_source: Eros and Civilization, Political Preface (1966); Marcuse is quoting a slogan, not coining one
suggested_refs: Das Ende der Utopie: Vortrage und Diskussionen in Berlin 1967

stops.name: Chalk Farm, the Roundhouse
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Congress on the Dialectics of Liberation, held at the Roundhouse in Camden from 15 to 30 July 1967, and for Marcuse's paper 'Liberation from the Affluent Society'. The exact day of his talk within the fortnight is not recorded; the date here is set inside the congress and should not be read as the day he spoke. Coordinate corrected to the building.
stops.campa: A converted railway engine shed in Camden, two weeks of it, an audience sitting on the floor. Gregory Bateson, R. D. Laing, Stokely Carmichael and Allen Ginsberg speak. Marcuse speaks too, in a suit, in the accent of a Berlin Gymnasium, arguing that the revolution now has to be made against a system that has already met the needs it created and against people who do not experience themselves as unfree. His paper is called Liberation from the Affluent Society. Which day of the fortnight he read it is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The Dialectics of Liberation, ed. David Cooper (Penguin, 1968), which prints the lecture

stops.name: Paris, the year of the revolt
stops.date_confidence: attested that Marcuse lectured repeatedly in Paris through the 1960s and engaged with the events of 1968; the specific movements of May 1968 are not fixed by any source consulted, and the month here orders the segment rather than fixing an appearance. Paris pin inherited from max_horkheimer.journey.json.
stops.campa: The students take the Latin Quarter, the factories stop, and for three weeks the French state does not know whether it still exists. His name is on the placards next to Marx and Mao. He has been coming to Paris to lecture since the early sixties and he comes again; what he says in private about the barricades is more careful than what the posters claim for him. The lecture he gives on the revolts survives only because a tape was kept in San Diego and someone transcribed it fifty years later.
stops.quote: If a state of affairs has come into existence where the masses are forced "into a life of toil and hunger, and obliged, in blood and tears, to maintain a handful of privileged beings in idleness and profligacy," then the social contract is abrogated, and the people can demand its restoration.
stops.quote_source: 'The Defense of Gracchus Babeuf Before the High Court of Vendome' (1969)
suggested_refs: Jacobin, 'Herbert Marcuse and the Student Revolts of 1968', printing the UCSD lecture

stops.name: San Diego, the governor and the guarded house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1968-1969 campaign against his employment, the death threats, and the university's refusal to dismiss him; the month is set to order the segment. The quote is from the Preface to An Essay on Liberation, published the following year.
stops.campa: Ronald Reagan, governor of California, joins the veterans' organizations and the local press in demanding that the state stop paying a Marxist to teach. Money is offered to buy out his contract and remove him from the payroll. Letters arrive promising to kill him. Students take turns sleeping at the house on the mesa. Colleagues stand watch through the nights. The campaign runs through 1968 and into 1969. The university refuses to dismiss him, and he goes on teaching.
stops.quote: The growing opposition to the global dominion of corporate capitalism is confronted by the sustained power of this dominion: its economic and military hold in the four continents, its neocolonial empire, and, most important, its unshaken capacity to subject the majority of the underlying population to its overwhelming productivity and force.
suggested_refs: CSUSM archival collection 'This Is an Order!' on the campaign against Marcuse

stops.name: San Diego, An Essay on Liberation
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1969; month not recorded and defaulted. The quote is verbatim from the Introduction, restored in full from the marxists.org text after an elided version circulated.
stops.campa: The shortest of his books and the least guarded. Against a lifetime of critical theory's refusal to describe the future, he describes it: a new sensibility, senses trained by something other than the market, needs that are not the needs installed by advertising, and a revolt in the colonized world that the metropolis cannot absorb because it does not run on the metropolis's satisfactions. He is writing at seventy-one about young people, from a mesa in California.
stops.quote: Up to now, it has been one of the principal tenets of the critical theory of society (and particularly Marxian theory) to refrain from what might be reasonably called utopian speculation.
suggested_refs: An Essay on Liberation (Beacon Press, 1969)

stops.name: San Diego, retirement and the defence of Angela Davis
stops.date_confidence: attested for the formal retirement in 1970 and for his public defence of Angela Davis after her 1970 arrest; she was acquitted in 1972. Months not recorded and set to order the segment. The quote is from his 1969 essay on Babeuf.
stops.campa: He retires formally and goes on teaching, lecturing and travelling as if nothing had been signed. In the same season his former Brandeis student Angela Davis is arrested, put on the federal fugitive list, and tried on capital charges; Marcuse defends her in public, in print, and by name. He had taught her Hegel and German idealism in Waltham a decade earlier. She is acquitted in 1972. What his name on her defence was worth inside the courtroom, nothing in the record measures.
stops.quote: consent obtained in this manner is annulled, is no consent, and government by the people must be achieved in the struggle against the people who consented to servitude.
stops.quote_source: 'The Defense of Gracchus Babeuf Before the High Court of Vendome' (1969)
suggested_refs: Logos Journal on Davis, Marcuse, critical theory and German idealism

segments.name: Counterrevolution and the Permanence of Art

stops.name: San Diego, Counterrevolution and Revolt, and the meaning of Chile
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1972 publication of Counterrevolution and Revolt; month defaulted. The Chile material, preserved by UCSD as 'The Meaning of Chile', follows the coup of 11 September 1973 and is [R] as to the exact occasion and audience.
stops.campa: The movements are ebbing and the reaction is organizing, and he writes a book that says so without consolation: the counterrevolution is preventive, it moves before the revolution it fears, and spontaneity is not a strategy. The next autumn the Chilean army bombs the presidential palace and Salvador Allende dies inside it, and Marcuse speaks about what it means that a socialism arrived at by ballot could be ended by aircraft. The talk survives in the San Diego archive under the title The Meaning of Chile.
suggested_refs: Counterrevolution and Revolt (Beacon Press, 1972)
'The Meaning of Chile', UCSD digital archive, library.ucsd.edu/dc/object/bb7953381x

stops.name: Starnberg, the Max Planck Institute
stops.date_confidence: attested for recurring lectures and discussions from 1974 at the Max Planck Institute for the Study of the Scientific-Technical World, where Jurgen Habermas was a director; month set to order the segment. The coordinate is the atlas's existing Starnberg pin, inherited byte-identical from gustav_landauer.journey.json, and stands for the town rather than the Institute's street address, which is not confirmed.
stops.campa: Every year now he crosses back to Bavaria, to a town south of Munich where a Max Planck institute studies what science and technology are doing to the conditions of life, and where Habermas is a director. Habermas thinks the Freudian theory of the instincts too speculative a foundation on which to build a politics. Marcuse will not give it up; without it there is no account of why people want what keeps them down. They respect each other and disagree in public, year after year, in a town on the Starnberger See.
suggested_refs: Max-Planck-Institut zur Erforschung der Lebensbedingungen der wissenschaftlich-technischen Welt, Starnberg
sources: Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews on Towards a Critical Theory of Society, ndpr.nd.edu

stops.name: La Jolla, the marriage to Erica Sherover
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the marcuse.org family page, which gives 21 June 1976 for the marriage to Erica Sherover, born 1938, died of cancer 15 December 1988. Inge Neumann Marcuse had died in 1973. The place of the ceremony is not documented; the coordinate stands for his residence.
stops.campa: Inge died in 1973. On the twenty-first of June he marries Erica Sherover, a philosopher who had been his student in San Diego and who is thirty-eight years younger than he is. She will outlive him by nine years and spend them building workshops on unlearning racism and internalized oppression, teaching under the name Sherover-Marcuse. It is his third marriage, and each of the three has been to a woman with work of her own. Where the ceremony took place is not documented. She dies of cancer in December 1988.
suggested_refs: Erica Sherover-Marcuse, Emancipation and Consciousness (1986), and her liberation-education workshops

stops.name: La Jolla, the permanence of art and the German autumn
stops.date_confidence: attested for both 1977 items: Die Permanenz der Kunst appeared that year, in English as The Aesthetic Dimension in 1978; 'Mord darf keine Waffe der Politik sein' appeared in Die Zeit on 23 September 1977, during the Schleyer kidnapping, not after 1968 as one dossier had it. The coordinate is his California residence; he moved between California and West Germany through this period.
stops.campa: Two pieces of writing in one year. The book argues that art is not the ideology of its class and cannot be judged by the politics of its author, and that a work's power to indict the world comes precisely from its refusal to resemble it. The newspaper article, printed in Die Zeit while the Red Army Faction holds a kidnapped industrialist and West Germany suspends its own rules to hunt them, says that murder must not be a weapon of politics. He defends counter-violence in self-defence and refuses terror.
suggested_refs: Die Permanenz der Kunst (1977), in English The Aesthetic Dimension (1978)
Mord darf keine Waffe der Politik sein, Die Zeit, 23 September 1977

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Romerberg
stops.date_confidence: attested that he spoke at the Frankfurt Romerberggesprache in the summer of 1979, his last public appearance, presenting theses on technology and society, and then travelled toward Starnberg. The exact day is not recorded; month set from the vita. Coordinate is the Frankfurt Romer pin already used in max_horkheimer.journey.json.
stops.campa: Eighty years old, he speaks in the old square of the city whose institute employed him for a lifetime and in which he never once worked a day, and sets out twenty-five theses on technology and society. Forty-six years earlier the same institute had put its money into Switzerland and its people onto trains. He has come back to the address he never had, to say what the machinery has done to the possibility of a different life. It is the last room he addresses. Afterwards he travels on toward Bavaria and the lake.
stops.quote: It is only for the sake of those without hope that hope is given to us.
stops.quote_source: One-Dimensional Man (1964), final line of chapter 10, quoting Walter Benjamin
suggested_refs: The Frankfurter Romerberggesprache of summer 1979

stops.name: Starnberg, the hospital by the lake
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the place of death; the sequence of the final illness, a heart ailment followed by a stroke, is [R], reconstructed from the vita and the encyclopaedia entries rather than from any medical record. No credible account suggests anything other than natural causes. Starnberg pin inherited from gustav_landauer.journey.json.
stops.campa: He dies in a hospital at Starnberg on the twenty-ninth of July, ten days after his eighty-first birthday, in the country he left in May 1933 and never lived in again. The heart goes first, then a stroke, though no medical record has been produced to say so. The body is cremated. What happens to the ashes then is not clear from any record: German accounts say they were simply forgotten, and no funeral home paper, no family letter, no cemetery register has been produced to say where they sat. They will sit there, wherever it is, for twenty-four years.
suggested_refs: The unresolved custody of the ashes, 1979-2003

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Nachlass at the Senckenberg library
stops.date_confidence: the 1984 deposit year rests on the Frankfurt university library's own archive record and was not independently corroborated; month defaulted. The coordinate is the Universitatsbibliothek Johann Christian Senckenberg at Freimannplatz 1, corrected from a point about a kilometre off.
stops.campa: His heirs deposit the papers, Na 3 Nachlass Herbert Marcuse, in the Frankfurt university library, and the city that never gave him a desk becomes the place where his handwriting is kept. The archive settles small questions with paper: which sections of the 1937 essay on philosophy and critical theory were his and which were Horkheimer's, for instance, a division the printed title page never made. Douglas Kellner begins editing the unpublished material into English volumes in 1998, and they keep coming for a decade and more.
suggested_refs: Na 3 Nachlass Herbert Marcuse, Universitatsbibliothek Johann Christian Senckenberg
Collected Papers of Herbert Marcuse, ed. Douglas Kellner, Routledge, from 1998

stops.name: Dorotheenstadtischer Friedhof, the one word on the stone
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the marcuse.org news and events page: interment on 18 July 2003 at the Dorotheenstadtischer Friedhof, Chausseestrasse 126, Berlin-Mitte, an Ehrengrab maintained by the city, with the stone designed by Bruno Flierl. The day before, the Free University held a symposium in his honour. The reading of the stone's form as a lectern and a figure 1 is [R] and unsupported by the sources retrieved.
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of July the ashes are put into the ground in Berlin-Mitte, twenty-four years after the death and a hundred and five years after the birth, four miles from the district where he went to school. The city gives him an honorary grave and pays for its upkeep. Bruno Flierl, an architecture critic and a friend of his son Peter, designs the stone. It carries no dates on its face and no titles, one word only, an imperative in the German he stopped writing his books in fifty years before: Weitermachen.
stops.quote_source: The inscription on Marcuse's gravestone, Dorotheenstadtischer Friedhof, Berlin
suggested_refs: The Berlin Ehrengraber of the Dorotheenstadtischer Friedhof, Chausseestrasse 126
sources: marcuse.org news and events page, marcuse.org/herbert/newsevents.htm
